literature.headline_en: Recent Lassa fever studies in Nigeria expose household risks, drug leads, and surveillance gaps.
literature.lead_en: Five studies released this window map community-level exposures, clinical delays, survivor sequelae, cross-state outbreak coordination, and a computational drug lead for Lassa virus in Nigeria.
key_findings_en: A four-state Nigerian survey (n=600) found 42% of households saw rodents daily or weekly and only 35% stored food in sealed containers, with rodent exposure and healthcare inaccessibility more pronounced in high-burden states, signalling a clear awareness-to-action gap [10.66837/ijphrad01/24/12].

Molecular docking and 100-ns MD simulations indicated Niloticin binds LASV GP2, SSP, and the nucleoprotein dTTP pocket with docking scores of −6.85, −7.17, and −7.36 kcal/mol, and MM/PBSA binding energies of approximately −62 to −100 kJ/mol, but antiviral activity remains unconfirmed [10.1038/s41598-026-64782-4].

In Ebonyi State (Dec 2024–Feb 2025), 10 laboratory-confirmed Lassa fever cases yielded a 40% CFR; 50% were initially treated for malaria or typhoid, and all deaths occurred in patients presenting ≥5 days after symptom onset [10.37432/jieph-d-26-00010].

A phenomenological study of 18 survivors in Southern Nigeria documented persistent weakness, hearing/vision difficulties, psychological distress, stigma, and occupational disruption beyond clinical discharge, underscoring the need for survivor-centred follow-up [10.9734/ajrid/2026/v17i9574].

Gombe State's 2024–2025 outbreak involved 11 confirmed cases and 6 deaths, with the index case imported from Taraba State; harmonisation across SORMAS, facility, and laboratory records plus IPC improvements halted further cases and healthcare worker infections [10.37432/jieph-d-26-00001].
literature.trend_or_risk_en: Persistent household rodent exposure, delayed care-seeking, and cross-state importation continue to drive Lassa fever burden in Nigeria, demanding integrated environmental, clinical, and interstate surveillance responses.
literature.caveats_en: Most included studies are descriptive, retrospective, or purely computational, with small samples and purposive sampling; experimental validation of Niloticin and larger prospective survivor cohorts are needed.
literature.brief_en: Five recent publications from Nigeria collectively highlight that Lassa fever transmission is sustained by household rodent exposure, food-storage gaps, and cross-state importation, while clinical outcomes are worsened by diagnostic delays and limited post-discharge support. A computational study identifies Niloticin as a multi-target LASV binder awaiting experimental confirmation, and field reports from Ebonyi and Gombe states reinforce the need for interstate data sharing, IPC strengthening, and survivor-centred care.

papers.title: Computational evaluation of Niloticin as a potential multi-target binder against Lassa virus glycoprotein and nucleoprotein
papers.abstract: Lassa fever is a potentially fatal disease with a high mortality rate and currently lacks an effective treatment, posing a significant threat, particularly in West Africa. In this study, Niloticin, a naturally occurring protolimonoid triterpenoid, was computationally evaluated as a potential multi-target binder against Lassa virus–associated host and viral targets using network pharmacology, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, hydrogen-bond occupancy analysis, and MM/PBSA binding-energy estimation. Eight overlapping candidate host-associated targets, namely F10, ABL1, AKT1, AR, BCHE, EGFR, KIT, and NLRP3, were identified using the GeneCards, OMIM, and SwissTargetPrediction databases. Functional enrichment analysis suggested possible associations with apoptosis, immune regulation, inflammation, coagulation, and cell-signaling pathways. Molecular docking predicted favorable binding of Niloticin to LASV glycoprotein regions GP2 and SSP, with docking scores of − 6.85 and − 7.17 kcal/mol, respectively, and to the nucleoprotein dTTP-binding pocket with a docking score of − 7.36 kcal/mol. Niloticin formed predicted hydrogen-bonding and hydrophobic interactions with key residues in GP2, SSP, and NP, including ARG422 and PHE434 in GP2, ALA25 and VAL18 in SSP, and residues surrounding the NP binding pocket. During MD simulations, Niloticin-bound systems exhibited comparatively stable trajectory behavior, as supported by RMSD, RMSF, radius of gyration, SASA, and hydrogen-bond analyses. Hydrogen-bond occupancy analysis further indicated recurrent ligand–protein contacts involving ARG422 in GP2, VAL18 and ALA25 in SSP, and THR178, GLU299, ARG323, and LYS253 in NP. MM/PBSA analysis showed favorable relative binding-energy estimates for Niloticin, ranging from approximately − 84 to − 100 kJ/mol for glycoprotein-associated systems and approximately − 62 kJ/mol for NP, mainly supported by van der Waals and nonpolar solvation contributions. Overall, these computational findings suggest that Niloticin may engage multiple LASV-associated viral and host targets and may be prioritized for further experimental investigation. However, the results are based entirely on computational analyses and do not confirm antiviral inhibition, direct host-target modulation, or functional blockade of LASV entry or replication. Experimental validation through cytotoxicity assays, biochemical binding studies, pseudovirus entry assays, and infectious-virus antiviral assays is required to establish the anti-LASV potential of Niloticin.

Eight overlapping candidate host-associated targets, namely F10, ABL1, AKT1, AR, BCHE, EGFR, KIT, and NLRP3, were identified using the GeneCards, OMIM, and SwissTargetPrediction databases. Functional enrichment analysis suggested possible associations with apoptosis, immune regulation, inflammation, coagulation, and cell-signaling pathways. Molecular docking predicted favorable binding of Niloticin to LASV glycoprotein regions GP2 and SSP, with docking scores of − 6.85 and − 7.17 kcal/mol, respectively, and to the nucleoprotein dTTP-binding pocket with a docking score of − 7.36 kcal/mol. Niloticin formed predicted hydrogen-bonding and hydrophobic interactions with key residues in GP2, SSP, and NP, including ARG422 and PHE434 in GP2, ALA25 and VAL18 in SSP, and residues surrounding the NP binding pocket. During MD simulations, Niloticin-bound systems exhibited comparatively stable trajectory behavior, as supported by RMSD, RMSF, radius of gyration, SASA, and hydrogen-bond analyses. Hydrogen-bond occupancy analysis further indicated recurrent ligand–protein contacts involving ARG422 in GP2, VAL18 and ALA25 in SSP, and THR178, GLU299, ARG323, and LYS253 in NP. MM/PBSA analysis showed favorable relative binding-energy estimates for Niloticin, ranging from approximately − 84 to − 100 kJ/mol for glycoprotein-associated systems and approximately − 62 kJ/mol for NP, mainly supported by van der Waals and nonpolar solvation contributions. Overall, these computational findings suggest that Niloticin may engage multiple LASV-associated viral and host targets and may be prioritized for further experimental investigation. However, the results are based entirely on computational analyses and do not confirm antiviral inhibition, direct host-target modulation, or functional blockade of LASV entry or replication. Experimental validation through cytotoxicity assays, biochemical binding studies, pseudovirus entry assays, and infectious-virus antiviral assays is required to establish the anti-LASV potential of Niloticin.

papers.title: Clinical and epidemiological characteristics of confirmed Lassa fever cases between December 2024 and February 2025 in Ebonyi State, Nigeria
papers.abstract: Introduction: Lassa Fever (LF) is an acute viral haemorrhagic illness endemic to West African countries. The disease remains a major public health concern in Nigeria and accounts for most reported global cases annually. Despite improvements in surveillance and case management, mortality remains high. Ebonyi State experiences recurrent outbreaks, yet limited case-level data exist to guide early detection and clinical response. Methods: A retrospective case series was conducted of laboratory-confirmed LF cases admitted at the designated LF treatment centre in Ebonyi State between December 2024 and February 2025. Data were extracted from hospital records, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) case investigation forms, and state surveillance line lists. The variables included demographic, clinical, and outcome characteristics. Descriptive statistics were summarised using medians and proportions. Results: Ten laboratory-confirmed cases were identified across multiple LGAs. The median age was 25.5 years (interquartile range: 18.8 – 29.0), and 60% were male. The most common presenting symptoms were fever, headache, and generalised weakness. Five of ten patients (50%) were initially treated for malaria or typhoid before LF was suspected. Severe complications, particularly bleeding and AKI, were observed more frequently among fatal cases. The overall case fatality rate was 40%, with all deaths occurring among patients presenting ≥5 days after symptom onset (median time to presentation: 7.5 days [fatal] versus 7.0 days [recovered]). Conclusion: Delayed presentation, initial misdiagnosis and severe complications were observed more frequently among fatal cases during the 2024–2025 LF transmission season in Ebonyi State. Early clinical suspicion, prompt referral, and timely initiation of Ribavirin and supportive care are likely important for improving survival, consistent with evidence from similar Lassa fever treatment settings in West Africa. Strengthening clinician awareness, diagnostic capacity, and community health-seeking behaviour remains essential to reducing LF-related mortality in endemic regions.

papers.title: Strengthening interstate surveillance and data sharing: Lessons from Gombe State’s Lassa fever outbreak response, Nigeria
papers.abstract: Introduction: Lassa fever (LF) endemicity in West Africa poses amplified risks due to population mobility and health system gaps. A LF outbreak in Gombe State, Nigeria (December 2024–February 2025), a non-hotspot state, exposed gaps in regional health security, interstate surveillance and coordination. The index case (a traveller from Taraba State) highlighted interstate border transmission risks. This study reviews Gombe State’s 2024/2025 LF outbreak data to strengthen LF outbreak control, enhance future outbreak preparedness and improve interstate collaboration. Methods: Nigeria’s National Rapid Response Team (NRRT) conducted a descriptive cross-sectional study of Gombe State LF cases between December 2024 and February 2025 across nine (82%) of the Local Government Areas (LGAs) from 12th to 26th February 2025. Response activities included active case search, retrospective record reviews, harmonisation of surveillance data using the Surveillance Outbreak Response Management and Analysis System (SORMAS), IPC assessments, environmental risk assessment, community engagement, and interstate coordination. Data were analysed descriptively by person, place, and time. Results: Thirty-nine suspected cases, 11 confirmed cases, one probable case, and six deaths were identified during the outbreak period. Imported cases linked to Taraba and Bauchi States contributed substantially to the outbreak. Surveillance data reconciliation improved harmonization of outbreak records across SORMAS, health facility records, laboratory records, and state line lists. IPC assessments identified gaps in triage systems, PPE utilisation, isolation capacity, and adherence to standard precautions. The objective of this study was to evaluate and compare household risk factors for Lassa fever transmission in two high-burden (Ondo and Edo) and two low-burden (Bauchi and Ebonyi) states in Nigeria. Four states (sample size determined by quota sampling) were purposively selected and each allocated 150 consenting adult respondents yielding an overall sample size of 600 respondents. Multistage stratified random sampling technique was employed. Data on fourteen variables were collected using a pre-tested structured questionnaire. The variables include; household history of LF; frequency of rodents per sighting; food storing habits; prevention practices against rodents; awareness about LF; accessibility to healthcare facilities; respondents who had ever attended health training; ever diagnosed with LF in the last five years; severity of symptoms; disease outcome; age distribution; respondents’ educational status; household hygiene level and hand washing practices among others. Responses for each independent variable were analysed using descriptive statistics and the results were presented based on states with high LF burden versus states with low LF burden. Among the respondents, 35.3% reported previous history of Lassa fever case in the household and 32.7% were not sure if they had a prior history of Lassa fever case. 42.0 percent of respondents reported seeing rodents daily or weekly in and around their households. Only 35.0% of households stored food in sealed containers. 36.7 percent practiced rodent preventive measures. 68.7 % reported that they had heard of Lassa fever prior to survey completion. Overall, there seemed to be gap between awareness of LF and taking preventative measures. 53.3 percent of participants reported challenges accessing health care. 53.3 percent of respondents reported that they had never participated in any health training about Lassa fever. 33.3% of the respondents have been diagnosed with Lassa fever in the past five years. Ten percent of respondents have had someone in their home die from Lassa fever. 46.7 % of respondents self-reported their hygiene practices as being either fair or poor. 30.0 percent of respondents stated that they always washed their hands. Those who responded from high burden states reported higher frequencies of rodent sightings, less frequent use of sealed storage containers, and more challenges with healthcare access when compared to respondents from low burden states. Persistent rodent exposure, unsafe food storage, low adoption of preventive measures, healthcare inaccessibility, and suboptimal hygiene are widespread across all four states and are more pronounced in high-burden states. A significant awareness-to-action gap indicates that knowledge alone is insufficient to change behaviour. Integrated community-level interventions addressing rodent control, food storage, health education outreach, and primary healthcare strengthening are urgently required and should be embedded within a One Health framework.

papers.title: Life after Lassa Fever: A Phenomenological Exploration of Survivors’ Lived Experiences in Southern Nigeria
papers.abstract: Background: Survival from Lassa fever may be followed by persistent physical symptoms, sensory difficulties, psychological distress, social disruption, and stigma. This study explored how survivors described the illness trajectory and life after treatment in Southern Nigeria. Methods: A qualitative phenomenological design was used. Eighteen purposively selected adults who had survived Lassa fever and had been clinically free of the acute illness for at least six months were recruited through three specialist treatment centres in Southern Nigeria. Data were generated through audio-recorded, semi-structured interviews and analysed thematically following Braun and Clarke’s framework. Results: The sample comprised 10 men and 8 women; 11 participants were aged 40 years or older, but two participants did not disclose their age. The accounts revealed delayed or missed diagnosis, severe physical suffering during the acute illness, emotional anguish, prolonged recovery, perceived hearing and visual difficulties, social and occupational disruption, stigma, isolation, deliberate concealment of diagnosis, and gratitude for survival and free treatment. Recovery was heterogeneous: some participants described progressive improvement, whereas others reported continuing weakness, pain, lethargy, or sensory difficulties. Conclusion: The outcome of the study indicates that recovery from Lassa fever extends beyond virological or clinical discharge. Survivor-centred follow-up should integrate the assessment of persistent physical and sensory symptoms, psychosocial support, stigma-reduction communication, and assistance with social and occupational reintegration. These findings are qualitative and should be interpreted within the context of the purposively selected sample.
